To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Hes1 gene, which encodes a protein that represses the expression of other genes, is required for the development of the extrahepatically located biliary system.
Hes1-deficiency causes conversion of biliary system into pancreatic tissue.
the biliary epithelial cells of Hes1-deficent mice ectopically express the proendocrine transcription factor Neurog3, and differentiate into pancreatic endocrine and excretory cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the liver, biliary system, and pancreas, and with the molecular basis for their development.
the molecular mechanisms that control cell and tissue differentiation during embryonic development.
the development of the biliopancreatic system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HES1 is a key factor that controls the differentiation of pancreatic and biliary epithelum.
the biliary system is a separate organ, and not part of the pancreas.
HES1 represses pancreatic development and promotes biliary development, and that the biliary system has the potential to develop into pancreatic tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the biliary system is plastic, and has the potential to be converted into other organ systems, including the pancreas.
HES1 is a master regulator of biliary development.
the biliary system and the pancreas are not two distinct organs but rather two different states of a single organ.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the biliary tree has a plasticity and can convert to pancreatic tissue.
the biliary epithelum has a plasticity to become pancreatic tissue, and that this is controlled by a single transcription factor, Hes1.
the biliary system is not an organ in its own right but a part of the pancreas.
